source: FLEURS dev transcripts, through bournemouth_aligner's std G2P
note: Accent marks on vowels (á, à, â, ǎ …) are pitch accents from the dictionaries of Slovenian and Lithuanian. They are separate tokens, but their boundaries are placed like those of the plain vowel.

SIL.name: silence
SIL.plain: A pause: no speech. Use it for a pause the speaker makes inside a segment.

noise.name: noise
noise.plain: A non-speech sound: a breath, cough, laugh or click.

<unk>.name: unknown
<unk>.plain: The G2P wrote a sound this model has no token for. Keep its time span; the label cannot say what it is.

s.name: voiceless alveolar fricative
s.plain: s. Also used for sˠ, which this model has no token of its own for

i.name: close front unrounded vowel
examples: k a t i k a

e.name: close-mid front unrounded vowel
e.plain: e as in Spanish or Italian “de”; the start of English “say”. Also used for eˀ, which this model has no token of its own for

n.name: alveolar nasal
n.plain: n. Also used for n̪ˠ, nˠ, which this model has no token of its own for

t.name: voiceless alveolar stop
t.plain: t as in “ten”. Also used for t̪ˠ, tˢ, which this model has no token of its own for

k.name: voiceless velar stop
examples: k a t i k a

o.name: close-mid back rounded vowel
o.plain: o as in Spanish or Italian “no”

m.name: bilabial nasal
m.plain: m. Also used for mˠ, which this model has no token of its own for

d.name: voiced alveolar stop
d.plain: d as in “dog”. Also used for d̥, d̪ˠ, which this model has no token of its own for

u.name: close back rounded vowel
u.plain: oo as in “food”. Also used for i͡u, which this model has no token of its own for

ɪ.name: near-close front unrounded vowel
ɪ.plain: i as in “sit”. Also used for ɜ͡ɪ, which this model has no token of its own for

ɾ.name: alveolar tap
ɾ.plain: one quick flap of the tongue, as in Spanish “pero”. Also used for ɾˠ, which this model has no token of its own for

f.name: voiceless labiodental fricative
f.plain: f. Also used for fˠ, which this model has no token of its own for

b.name: voiced bilabial stop
b.plain: b as in “bed”. Also used for b̥, ɓ, bˠ, which this model has no token of its own for

w.name: labial-velar approximant
w.plain: w as in “we”. Also used for wˀ, which this model has no token of its own for

ɑ.name: open back unrounded vowel
ɑ.plain: a as in “father”. Also used for ɑˀ, ɑ͡ɪ, which this model has no token of its own for

ɡ.name: voiced velar stop
ɡ.plain: g as in “go”. Also used for ɡ̥, which this model has no token of its own for

ʔ.name: glottal stop
ʔ.plain: the catch in the throat in “uh-oh”

ɔ.name: open-mid back rounded vowel
ɔ.plain: o as in British “thought”. Also used for ɔˀ, which this model has no token of its own for

ʊ.name: near-close back rounded vowel
ʊ.plain: oo as in “book”. Also used for ə͡ʊ, which this model has no token of its own for

ɯ.name: close back unrounded vowel
examples: f a r k ɫ ɯ
j a ɾ ɯ ʃ ɯ n ɯ
k ɛ m t s ɯ

ʁ.name: voiced uvular fricative
ʁ.plain: the r of French and German. Also used for ʁ̥, which this model has no token of its own for

ɐ.name: near-open central vowel
ɐ.plain: a short, relaxed “uh” (Portuguese “cama”, German “-er” endings). Also used for ɐ̯ˀ, which this model has no token of its own for

ð.name: voiced dental fricative
ð.plain: th as in “this”. Also used for ðˀ, ð̩, which this model has no token of its own for

æ.name: near-open front unrounded vowel
æ.plain: a as in “cat”. Also used for æˀ, which this model has no token of its own for

β.name: voiced bilabial fricative
β.plain: a soft b where the lips do not close (Spanish b between vowels)

ɫ.name: velarised alveolar lateral
examples: o ɫ a ɾ a k
b o ɫ ɡ æ n

q.name: voiceless uvular stop
q.plain: a k made further back, at the uvula (Uzbek “q”)
examples: v e l ɑ s q u e z

ʂ.name: voiceless retroflex fricative
ʂ.plain: a hard sh with the tongue tip back (Polish “sz”)

ɣ.name: voiced velar fricative
ɣ.plain: a g where the tongue does not close (Dutch g, Spanish g between vowels)
examples: s ɔ m ə ɣ ə
a l ɣ u ŋ s

y.name: close front rounded vowel
y.plain: ee said with rounded lips (French “tu”, German “über”)

ɨ.name: close central unrounded vowel
ɨ.plain: between ee and oo, lips spread (Polish “y”, Welsh “u”). Also used for ɨ̯, ɨ̞, which this model has no token of its own for

ʕ.name: voiced pharyngeal fricative
ʕ.plain: a voiced throat sound (Arabic ع). Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

ħ.name: voiceless pharyngeal fricative
ħ.plain: a strong h squeezed in the throat (Arabic ح). Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

ɕ.name: voiceless alveolo-palatal fricative
ɕ.plain: a soft sh, with the tongue body raised (Polish “ś”)
examples: ɔ f i ɕ ɛ l ə

ɳ.name: retroflex nasal
ɳ.plain: n with the tongue tip curled back
examples: f ɔ ʂ k a ɳ a
f ɔ ʂ k ə ɳ ə

ɵ.name: close-mid central rounded vowel
ɵ.plain: a rounded vowel between e and o (Swedish short u)
examples: ɡ r u ɵ n d

t͡s.name: voiceless alveolar affricate
examples: t͡s i t͡s a w t͡s e

ʏ.name: near-close front rounded vowel
ʏ.plain: i as in “sit” said with rounded lips (German “hübsch”)

ø.name: close-mid front rounded vowel
ø.plain: e said with rounded lips (German “schön”, French “peu”). Also used for øˀ, which this model has no token of its own for
examples: k y l ø m b ø z ø

œ.name: open-mid front rounded vowel
œ.plain: e as in “bed” said with rounded lips (French “neuf”, German “können”). Also used for ɶ, which this model has no token of its own for

ʉ.name: close central rounded vowel
ʉ.plain: a rounded vowel between ee and oo (Norwegian and Swedish “du”)

tʲ.name: voiceless alveolar stop, palatalised
tʲ.plain: t as in “ten”; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)

lʲ.name: alveolar lateral approximant, palatalised
lʲ.plain: l as in “leaf”; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)

sʲ.name: voiceless alveolar fricative, palatalised
sʲ.plain: s; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)
examples: ʋ a lʲ sʲ tʲ ɪ j o sʲ ɛ
p u t e t sʲ
ʃ ɪ n̠ʲ sʲ ə ɾʲ

nʲ.name: alveolar nasal, palatalised
nʲ.plain: n; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)

ɑ̃.name: open back unrounded vowel, nasalised
ɑ̃.plain: a as in “father”; nasalised: air also flows through the nose (French “an”, Portuguese “não”)
examples: b l ɑ̃ d a d

ʎ.name: palatal lateral approximant
ʎ.plain: an l made with the tongue body, close to “ly” (Italian “gli”)

ɒ.name: open back rounded vowel
ɒ.plain: a rounded “ah” (British “lot”, Hungarian “a”). Also used for ɒˀ, which this model has no token of its own for
examples: k ɒ m ə n w ɛ l θ

ʈ.name: voiceless retroflex stop
ʈ.plain: t with the tongue tip curled back (Swedish and Norwegian “rt”)
examples: f ʉ l f œ ʈ ə

rʲ.name: alveolar trill, palatalised
rʲ.plain: a rolled r; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)
examples: ɲ i ɡ ɛ rʲ j i

t͡ʃ.name: voiceless postalveolar affricate
examples: f ɾ e k w ẽ t͡ʃ i m ẽ t͡ʃ i
t͡ʃ ɛ p r á ʋ

tʰ.name: voiceless alveolar stop, aspirated
tʰ.plain: t as in “ten”; aspirated: followed by a puff of breath before the vowel starts (English “top” has one, “stop” does not)
examples: tʰ ɪ l p a k a

ɐ̯.name: near-open central vowel, non-syllabic
ɐ̯.plain: a short, relaxed “uh” (Portuguese “cama”, German “-er” endings); non-syllabic: the weak, glide-like half of a diphthong; it is not a syllable on its own
examples: ʔ a n v ɛ n d ɐ̯

ɔ̯.name: open-mid back rounded vowel, non-syllabic
ɔ̯.plain: o as in British “thought”; non-syllabic: the weak, glide-like half of a diphthong; it is not a syllable on its own
examples: ẽ i t ʁ ɑ ɔ̯ d͡z ʏ s ə ʁ a d

t̪.name: voiceless alveolar stop, dental
t̪.plain: t as in “ten”; dental: the tongue tip touches the upper teeth
examples: a β i t a̝ t̪

c.name: voiceless palatal stop
c.plain: a k made against the hard palate, close to “ty” (Hungarian “ty”, Czech “ť”)

ɭ.name: retroflex lateral approximant
ɭ.plain: l with the tongue tip curled back
examples: k ɛ r ɭ e k e n s
n ø ð b e s d ɛ m ɭ s ə

mʲ.name: bilabial nasal, palatalised
mʲ.plain: m; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)

ɔ̃.name: open-mid back rounded vowel, nasalised
ɔ̃.plain: o as in British “thought”; nasalised: air also flows through the nose (French “an”, Portuguese “não”)
examples: ɛ̃ f ɔ ʁ m a s j ɔ̃

ç.name: voiceless palatal fricative
ç.plain: the ch of German “ich”; like a strong h before ee

õ.name: close-mid back rounded vowel, nasalised
õ.plain: o as in Spanish or Italian “no”; nasalised: air also flows through the nose (French “an”, Portuguese “não”)

ʐ.name: voiced retroflex fricative
examples: ɔ ɡ a ʐ ɨ n s k a

vʲ.name: voiced labiodental fricative, palatalised
vʲ.plain: v; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)
examples: vʲ ɛ ŋ k ʂ ɔ ɕ t͡ɕ

d͡ʒ.name: voiced postalveolar affricate
examples: m ə n d͡ʒ a d i

kʰ.name: voiceless velar stop, aspirated
kʰ.plain: k as in “key”; aspirated: followed by a puff of breath before the vowel starts (English “top” has one, “stop” does not)
examples: n a u kʰ v a i m a r ɪ
kʰ v ɪ n ɔ r

ʀ.name: uvular trill
ʀ.plain: an r rolled at the uvula (Luxembourgish r)
examples: ɡ ʀ æ n z ə n

ă.name: open front unrounded vowel, extra-short
ă.plain: a as in Spanish “casa”; extra-short: a very short version of the vowel

dʲ.name: voiced alveolar stop, palatalised
dʲ.plain: d as in “dog”; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)

ɖ.name: voiced retroflex stop
ɖ.plain: d with the tongue tip curled back (Swedish and Norwegian “rd”)

ʑ.name: voiced alveolo-palatal fricative
examples: vʲ ɛ̃ ʑ ɲ u f
ʑ i d v ə ʀ e n

pʲ.name: voiceless bilabial stop, palatalised
pʲ.plain: p as in “pen”; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)
examples: tʲ i mʲ pʲ ə l

ʋ.name: labiodental approximant
ʋ.plain: a soft v without friction (Dutch w, Slovenian v)

pʰ.name: voiceless bilabial stop, aspirated
pʰ.plain: p as in “pen”; aspirated: followed by a puff of breath before the vowel starts (English “top” has one, “stop” does not)

kʲ.name: voiceless velar stop, palatalised
kʲ.plain: k as in “key”; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants). Also used for kʲ̩, which this model has no token of its own for
examples: kʲ ɪ t o kʲ u
a f r ɨ kʲ i

s̠.name: voiceless alveolar fricative, retracted
s̠.plain: s; retracted: made a little further back in the mouth. Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

d̪.name: voiced alveolar stop, dental
d̪.plain: d as in “dog”; dental: the tongue tip touches the upper teeth

d͡ʑ.name: voiced alveolo-palatal affricate
examples: b a r d͡ʑ ɛ j
i z m ɛ d͡ʑ ʊ

o̞.name: close-mid back rounded vowel, lowered
o̞.plain: o as in Spanish or Italian “no”; lowered: a little more open; a lowered fricative is a smooth approximant with no friction. Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

bʲ.name: voiced bilabial stop, palatalised
bʲ.plain: b as in “bed”; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)

ɟ.name: voiced palatal stop
ɟ.plain: a g made against the hard palate, close to “dy” (Hungarian “gy”, Czech “ď”). Also used for ʄ, which this model has no token of its own for

ẽ.name: close-mid front unrounded vowel, nasalised
ẽ.plain: e as in Spanish or Italian “de”; the start of English “say”; nasalised: air also flows through the nose (French “an”, Portuguese “não”)
examples: ẽ i f l y ə ʁ a d

d͡z.name: voiced alveolar affricate
examples: u t i l i d d͡z a
u t i l i d͡z a n

ɦ.name: voiced glottal fricative
ɦ.plain: a breathy, voiced h (Dutch and Czech h)

ʝ.name: voiced palatal fricative
examples: k ɾ u ʝ e ɾ

ɥ.name: labial-palatal approximant
examples: p ʁ ɔ d ɥ i
s i t ɥ a s j ɔ̃

i̯.name: close front unrounded vowel, non-syllabic
i̯.plain: ee as in “see”; non-syllabic: the weak, glide-like half of a diphthong; it is not a syllable on its own
examples: p o d i̯ ʊ m

ɛ̃.name: open-mid front unrounded vowel, nasalised
ɛ̃.plain: e as in “bed”; nasalised: air also flows through the nose (French “an”, Portuguese “não”)

zʲ.name: voiced alveolar fricative, palatalised
zʲ.plain: z; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)
examples: p ɐ ʋʲ i zʲ dʲ ʒʲ ʊ ɪ
a p e l e zʲ

o̝.name: close-mid back rounded vowel, raised
o̝.plain: o as in Spanish or Italian “no”; raised: a little closer (tongue higher) than the plain symbol

n̪.name: alveolar nasal, dental
n̪.plain: n; dental: the tongue tip touches the upper teeth

ɛ̝.name: open-mid front unrounded vowel, raised
ɛ̝.plain: e as in “bed”; raised: a little closer (tongue higher) than the plain symbol
examples: ʌ m k ʁ ɛ̝ ŋ

ɡʲ.name: voiced velar stop, palatalised
ɡʲ.plain: g as in “go”; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)
examples: d ɐ ʊ ɡʲ ɛ lʲ ɪ s
t ɛ x n ɔ l ɔ ɡʲ j i

ǎ.name: open front unrounded vowel, accent ˇ (rising)
ǎ.plain: a as in Spanish “casa”; accent ˇ (rising): the G2P's dictionary marks a rising pitch accent. Also used for ä̌, which this model has no token of its own for

æ̃.name: near-open front unrounded vowel, nasalised
æ̃.plain: a as in “cat”; nasalised: air also flows through the nose (French “an”, Portuguese “não”). Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

u̯.name: close back rounded vowel, non-syllabic
u̯.plain: oo as in “food”; non-syllabic: the weak, glide-like half of a diphthong; it is not a syllable on its own

ã.name: open front unrounded vowel, nasalised
ã.plain: a as in Spanish “casa”; nasalised: air also flows through the nose (French “an”, Portuguese “não”). Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

fʲ.name: voiceless labiodental fricative, palatalised
fʲ.plain: f; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)
examples: a fʲ rʲ ɪ k o s

a͡ɪ.name: diphthong a to ɪ
examples: s ə b a ɡ a͡ɪ

r̥.name: alveolar trill, voiceless
r̥.plain: a rolled r; voiceless: said without vocal-fold vibration, as if whispered
examples: f ɪ r̥ s t ʏ
s t œ r̥ s t a

s̺.name: voiceless alveolar fricative, apical
s̺.plain: s; apical: made with the very tip of the tongue. Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

ɫ̪.name: velarised alveolar lateral, dental
ɫ̪.plain: the dark l of “full”; dental: the tongue tip touches the upper teeth. Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

l̪.name: alveolar lateral approximant, dental
l̪.plain: l as in “leaf”; dental: the tongue tip touches the upper teeth. Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

χ.name: voiceless uvular fricative
χ.plain: a rougher ch made at the uvula (Welsh “ch”)
examples: ɡ i ŋ r i χ

s̻.name: voiceless alveolar fricative, laminal
s̻.plain: s; laminal: made with the blade of the tongue, just behind the tip. Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

î.name: close front unrounded vowel, accent ˆ (falling)
î.plain: ee as in “see”; accent ˆ (falling): the G2P's dictionary marks a falling pitch accent
examples: ɾ ɐ ʃʲ î tʲ ɪ

ɽ.name: retroflex flap
ɽ.plain: a flap with the tongue tip curled back
examples: l ʉ d ʋ ɪ k æ ɽ ə l s

á.name: open front unrounded vowel, accent ´ (high)
á.plain: a as in Spanish “casa”; accent ´ (high): the G2P's dictionary marks a pitch accent or stress here

é.name: close-mid front unrounded vowel, accent ´ (high)
é.plain: e as in Spanish or Italian “de”; the start of English “say”; accent ´ (high): the G2P's dictionary marks a pitch accent or stress here

ó.name: close-mid back rounded vowel, accent ´ (high)
ó.plain: o as in Spanish or Italian “no”; accent ´ (high): the G2P's dictionary marks a pitch accent or stress here

ĭ.name: close front unrounded vowel, extra-short
ĭ.plain: ee as in “see”; extra-short: a very short version of the vowel
examples: p o p u l ɑ t s ĭ o n
f ɾ ɪ k t s ĭ o n ə n

ʃʲ.name: voiceless postalveolar fricative, palatalised
ʃʲ.plain: sh as in “ship”; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)
examples: t a tʲ ʃʲ ɛ ʊ̯

â.name: open front unrounded vowel, accent ˆ (falling)
â.plain: a as in Spanish “casa”; accent ˆ (falling): the G2P's dictionary marks a falling pitch accent

s̪.name: voiceless alveolar fricative, dental
s̪.plain: s; dental: the tongue tip touches the upper teeth

í.name: close front unrounded vowel, accent ´ (high)
í.plain: ee as in “see”; accent ´ (high): the G2P's dictionary marks a pitch accent or stress here

tʼ.name: voiceless alveolar stop, ejective
tʼ.plain: t as in “ten”; ejective: a pop made by the throat, with no breath from the lungs. Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

r̩.name: alveolar trill, syllabic
r̩.plain: a rolled r; syllabic: forms a syllable with no vowel, as the n of “button”

xʲ.name: voiceless velar fricative, palatalised
xʲ.plain: ch as in Scottish “loch”, German “Bach”; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)
examples: xʲ i ʂ p a ɲ ɛ
mʲ ɪ xʲ ɛ lʲ ɛ

ĩ.name: close front unrounded vowel, nasalised
ĩ.plain: ee as in “see”; nasalised: air also flows through the nose (French “an”, Portuguese “não”)

ɜ.name: open-mid central unrounded vowel
ɜ.plain: like the vowel of British “bird”. Also used for ɜ͡ɪ, which this model has no token of its own for
examples: b ɔ f a l o pʰ i d s b ɜ

o͡ʊ.name: diphthong o to ʊ
examples: p o m o t͡s o͡ʊ

l̥.name: alveolar lateral approximant, voiceless
l̥.plain: l as in “leaf”; voiceless: said without vocal-fold vibration, as if whispered

ô.name: close-mid back rounded vowel, accent ˆ (falling)
ô.plain: o as in Spanish or Italian “no”; accent ˆ (falling): the G2P's dictionary marks a falling pitch accent

ɐ̃.name: near-open central vowel, nasalised
ɐ̃.plain: a short, relaxed “uh” (Portuguese “cama”, German “-er” endings); nasalised: air also flows through the nose (French “an”, Portuguese “não”)

kʼ.name: voiceless velar stop, ejective
kʼ.plain: k as in “key”; ejective: a pop made by the throat, with no breath from the lungs. Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

a̯.name: open front unrounded vowel, non-syllabic
a̯.plain: a as in Spanish “casa”; non-syllabic: the weak, glide-like half of a diphthong; it is not a syllable on its own. Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

ʊ̃.name: near-close back rounded vowel, nasalised
ʊ̃.plain: oo as in “book”; nasalised: air also flows through the nose (French “an”, Portuguese “não”). Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

l̠.name: alveolar lateral approximant, retracted
l̠.plain: l as in “leaf”; retracted: made a little further back in the mouth. Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

cʰ.name: voiceless palatal stop, aspirated
cʰ.plain: a k made against the hard palate, close to “ty” (Hungarian “ty”, Czech “ť”); aspirated: followed by a puff of breath before the vowel starts (English “top” has one, “stop” does not)
examples: cʰ ɪ k l i ŋ d ʏ n

à.name: open front unrounded vowel, accent ` (low)
à.plain: a as in Spanish “casa”; accent ` (low): the G2P's dictionary marks a pitch accent or stress here

ɪ̯.name: near-close front unrounded vowel, non-syllabic
ɪ̯.plain: i as in “sit”; non-syllabic: the weak, glide-like half of a diphthong; it is not a syllable on its own

e̯.name: close-mid front unrounded vowel, non-syllabic
e̯.plain: e as in Spanish or Italian “de”; the start of English “say”; non-syllabic: the weak, glide-like half of a diphthong; it is not a syllable on its own. Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

y̯.name: close front rounded vowel, non-syllabic
y̯.plain: ee said with rounded lips (French “tu”, German “über”); non-syllabic: the weak, glide-like half of a diphthong; it is not a syllable on its own

n̥.name: alveolar nasal, voiceless
n̥.plain: n; voiceless: said without vocal-fold vibration, as if whispered
examples: n̥ a h k a r
ʏ h p m ʏ n̥ t r a n d ə

l̩.name: alveolar lateral approximant, syllabic
l̩.plain: l as in “leaf”; syllabic: forms a syllable with no vowel, as the n of “button”

ɬ.name: voiceless alveolar lateral fricative
ɬ.plain: the Welsh “ll”: an l blown without voice

ʋʲ.name: labiodental approximant, palatalised
ʋʲ.plain: a soft v without friction (Dutch w, Slovenian v); palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)

ɾʲ.name: alveolar tap, palatalised
ɾʲ.plain: one quick flap of the tongue, as in Spanish “pero”; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)
examples: ʋ ɐ ɾʲ ʒʲ i b o s

t̪ʰ.name: voiceless alveolar stop, dental, aspirated
t̪ʰ.plain: t as in “ten”; dental: the tongue tip touches the upper teeth; aspirated: followed by a puff of breath before the vowel starts (English “top” has one, “stop” does not). Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

ŋ̩.name: velar nasal, syllabic
ŋ̩.plain: ng as in “sing”; syllabic: forms a syllable with no vowel, as the n of “button”

ɰ.name: velar approximant
ɰ.plain: a g so weak the tongue never closes
examples: p ɐ m ɐ m ɐ ɰ i t ɐ n

a̝.name: open front unrounded vowel, raised
a̝.plain: a as in Spanish “casa”; raised: a little closer (tongue higher) than the plain symbol

ɻ.name: retroflex approximant
ɻ.plain: an English-like r with the tongue tip curled back

ʍ.name: voiceless labial-velar approximant
ʍ.plain: a breathy w (“wh” in some accents)
examples: ʍ i l a j a

ũ.name: close back rounded vowel, nasalised
ũ.plain: oo as in “food”; nasalised: air also flows through the nose (French “an”, Portuguese “não”)

m̩.name: bilabial nasal, syllabic
m̩.plain: m; syllabic: forms a syllable with no vowel, as the n of “button”
examples: s m̩ ɲ ɛ n u
k m̩ t v o ɾ i k t s i

r̝.name: alveolar trill, raised
r̝.plain: a rolled r; raised: a little closer (tongue higher) than the plain symbol
examples: r̝ ɛ ʃ ɛ ɲ i

w̃.name: labial-velar approximant, nasalised
w̃.plain: w as in “we”; nasalised: air also flows through the nose (French “an”, Portuguese “não”)

n̩.name: alveolar nasal, syllabic
n̩.plain: n; syllabic: forms a syllable with no vowel, as the n of “button”

ì.name: close front unrounded vowel, accent ` (low)
ì.plain: ee as in “see”; accent ` (low): the G2P's dictionary marks a pitch accent or stress here

ʊ̯.name: near-close back rounded vowel, non-syllabic
ʊ̯.plain: oo as in “book”; non-syllabic: the weak, glide-like half of a diphthong; it is not a syllable on its own
examples: t a tʲ ʃʲ ɛ ʊ̯

ʒʲ.name: voiced postalveolar fricative, palatalised
ʒʲ.plain: s as in “measure”; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)
examples: p ɐ ʋʲ i zʲ dʲ ʒʲ ʊ ɪ

n̠ʲ.name: alveolar nasal, retracted, palatalised
n̠ʲ.plain: n; retracted: made a little further back in the mouth; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)

ɱ.name: labiodental nasal
ɱ.plain: m made with the lower lip against the teeth, before f or v (“comfort”)
examples: ɱ a ɾ e k a n i
i ɱ f o ɾ m a θ j o ŋ
k y l ø ɱ f e l ɛ

qʼ.name: voiceless uvular stop, ejective
qʼ.plain: a k made further back, at the uvula (Uzbek “q”); ejective: a pop made by the throat, with no breath from the lungs. Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

t͡ʃʼ.name: ejective postalveolar affricate
t͡ʃʼ.plain: ch said with a pop from the throat, no breath. Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

è.name: close-mid front unrounded vowel, accent ` (low)
è.plain: e as in Spanish or Italian “de”; the start of English “say”; accent ` (low): the G2P's dictionary marks a pitch accent or stress here

ŋ̥.name: velar nasal, voiceless
ŋ̥.plain: ng as in “sing”; voiceless: said without vocal-fold vibration, as if whispered
examples: ɛ ŋ̥ r a i̯ f d

m̥.name: bilabial nasal, voiceless
m̥.plain: m; voiceless: said without vocal-fold vibration, as if whispered

ú.name: close back rounded vowel, accent ´ (high)
ú.plain: oo as in “food”; accent ´ (high): the G2P's dictionary marks a pitch accent or stress here

kʷ.name: voiceless velar stop, labialised
kʷ.plain: k as in “key”; labialised: said with rounded lips. Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

ò.name: close-mid back rounded vowel, accent ` (low)
ò.plain: o as in Spanish or Italian “no”; accent ` (low): the G2P's dictionary marks a pitch accent or stress here
examples: ɔ b m ò t͡ʃ i j

ù.name: close back rounded vowel, accent ` (low)
ù.plain: oo as in “food”; accent ` (low): the G2P's dictionary marks a pitch accent or stress here

o̯.name: close-mid back rounded vowel, non-syllabic
o̯.plain: o as in Spanish or Italian “no”; non-syllabic: the weak, glide-like half of a diphthong; it is not a syllable on its own

l̠ʲ.name: alveolar lateral approximant, retracted, palatalised
l̠ʲ.plain: l as in “leaf”; retracted: made a little further back in the mouth; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)

e̝.name: close-mid front unrounded vowel, raised
e̝.plain: e as in Spanish or Italian “de”; the start of English “say”; raised: a little closer (tongue higher) than the plain symbol

j̃.name: palatal approximant, nasalised
j̃.plain: y as in “yes”; nasalised: air also flows through the nose (French “an”, Portuguese “não”)

ɛ́.name: open-mid front unrounded vowel, accent ´ (high)
ɛ́.plain: e as in “bed”; accent ´ (high): the G2P's dictionary marks a pitch accent or stress here

ɔ́.name: open-mid back rounded vowel, accent ´ (high)
ɔ́.plain: o as in British “thought”; accent ´ (high): the G2P's dictionary marks a pitch accent or stress here

ɔ̀.name: open-mid back rounded vowel, accent ` (low)
ɔ̀.plain: o as in British “thought”; accent ` (low): the G2P's dictionary marks a pitch accent or stress here
examples: s k ɔ̀ r a j

e͡ʊ.name: diphthong e to ʊ
e͡ʊ.plain: e gliding to oo. Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

ɛ̀.name: open-mid front unrounded vowel, accent ` (low)
ɛ̀.plain: e as in “bed”; accent ` (low): the G2P's dictionary marks a pitch accent or stress here

œ̃.name: open-mid front rounded vowel, nasalised
œ̃.plain: e as in “bed” said with rounded lips (French “neuf”, German “können”); nasalised: air also flows through the nose (French “an”, Portuguese “não”)

ɑ̯.name: open back unrounded vowel, non-syllabic
ɑ̯.plain: a as in “father”; non-syllabic: the weak, glide-like half of a diphthong; it is not a syllable on its own. Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

ɘ.name: close-mid central unrounded vowel
ɘ.plain: a schwa-like vowel, a little higher than ə. Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

ŋʲ.name: velar nasal, palatalised
ŋʲ.plain: ng as in “sing”; palatalised: said with the tongue body raised toward the palate: a y-like colour (“soft” consonants)
examples: ɪ ʃʲ ʋʲ ɛ ŋʲ kʲ tʲ ɪ

ð̞.name: voiced dental fricative, lowered
ð̞.plain: th as in “this”; lowered: a little more open; a lowered fricative is a smooth approximant with no friction. Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language

β̞.name: voiced bilabial fricative, lowered
β̞.plain: a soft b where the lips do not close (Spanish b between vowels); lowered: a little more open; a lowered fricative is a smooth approximant with no friction. Rare: not in the test sentences of any trained language
